title: Do regulatory sandboxes help UK fintechs, or just make good headlines?
label: Regulatory sandboxes · Fintech
summary: Witnesses from start-up and scale-up fintechs told the committee that UK sandboxes have some uses but are not the main driver of fintech success. They described sandboxes as costly, confusing, and often better suited to large incumbents than small innovators. The witnesses recommended faster authorisation, clearer paths out of sandboxes, provisional licences for limited real‑world trading, technical benchmarking, and learning from better-executed programmes overseas.

glossary.definition: A controlled testing environment where firms can try new financial products with some regulatory oversight and possibly temporary waivers.
Financial Conduct Authority, the UK regulator for financial services.
Office of Fair Trading, the earlier regulator that supervised some lenders before the FCA existed.
Formal permission from the FCA allowing a firm to operate in regulated financial activities.
The FCA staff member assigned to handle a firm's authorisation or regulatory case.
A suggested limited, supervised permission to trade while full authorisation is being processed.
An FCA sandbox variant that gives participants extra tools such as computing power and synthetic data for testing.
A type of digital token intended to keep a stable value, often backed by assets or other mechanisms.

chapters.title: Opening: what sandboxes actually do
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said sandboxes help in narrow cases but are not a main reason for UK fintech success; authorisation speed and access to capital and talent matter more.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are looking at regulatory sandboxes. How important have they been to UK fintech success, and should entry be easier or should other approaches be used?

turns.speaker: Sebastian McDermott
turns.text: Sandboxes have helped in places, but things like capital and talent are bigger factors. They're not in my top ten drivers of success.

turns.speaker: Chris Bosworth
turns.text: From a consumer-lending view, many successful firms grew before sandboxes existed under the OFT, which had a lower bar than the FCA. Sandboxes often suit larger firms—not bootstrapped start-ups.

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: We were authorised without using the sandbox. For our business—building a credit bureau—you need full, open-market data-sharing, which a sandbox can't deliver.

turns.speaker: Oliver Quie
turns.text: Our device-authentication firm didn't use a UK sandbox; we found more useful technical evaluation abroad. Sandboxes should enable technical benchmarking, not just paperwork.

chapters.title: Practical barriers: cost, clarity and pathways
chapters.takeaway: Start-ups find sandboxes expensive, time-consuming and unclear about how to progress to full authorisation.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: How should sandbox performance be measured?

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: Measure whether sandboxes produce clear routes to authorisation. For us, the sandbox was not compatible with the multi-party data sharing a credit bureau needs.

turns.speaker: Oliver Quie
turns.text: There should be objective technical metrics in sandboxes so vendors are judged by performance, not reputation. That would level the playing field.

turns.speaker: Chris Bosworth
turns.text: Metrics should include how many participants progress to authorisation, and also how many the sandbox correctly filters out. But resources are limited, so ask about return on investment.

turns.speaker: Lord Hollick
turns.text: Why did your firm not use the sandbox for car-finance lending?

turns.speaker: Chris Bosworth
turns.text: The sandbox application was as arduous and costly as full authorisation. As a small start-up we chose direct authorisation; for us it was faster and more sensible.

turns.speaker: Lord Turnbull
turns.text: What actually happens once a firm is in a sandbox—how do they exit?

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: That's the problem: the exit path is unclear. You may have to reapply for full authorisation with no guarantee. Firms need a defined checklist like development sandboxes have.

turns.speaker: Lord Turnbull
turns.text: Has there been a proper review of sandboxes?

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: Not recently—last major review was years ago. The FCA should run retrospectives: cohort outcomes, who benefited, and how to improve.

turns.speaker: Sebastian McDermott
turns.text: If the goal is authorisation, that's already a separate FCA job. Sandboxes are better used where activity sits outside the current regulatory perimeter.

chapters.title: How sandboxes could be reformed
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses proposed speeding up authorisation, provisional licences for limited real trading, technical benchmarks, clearer oversight and learning from overseas programmes.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bowles of Berkhamsted
turns.text: Who benefits from sandboxes—the regulator, firms or consumers?

turns.speaker: Sebastian McDermott
turns.text: There are good use cases: testing things outside the perimeter. But if sandboxes become a side-channel for authorisation, they confuse resource allocation.

turns.speaker: Chris Bosworth
turns.text: I favour provisional licensing: let start-ups trade at small scale under supervision to prove market fit and build revenue, rather than opaque sandbox tests with synthetic data.

turns.speaker: Lord Eatwell
turns.text: What practical steps would reduce regulatory risk for innovators?

turns.speaker: Sebastian McDermott
turns.text: Speed the core authorisation process—cut months off waiting times. Faster decisions reduce cash burn and investor uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: Trust applicants more initially and take enforcement away if they later break rules. The process felt like 'guilty until proven innocent'; reverse that where safe.

turns.speaker: Oliver Quie
turns.text: Introduce technical benchmarking and clear objective success criteria in sandboxes. Regulators are best placed to set those criteria objectively.

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: How would provisional licensing handle consumer compensation if things go wrong?

turns.speaker: Chris Bosworth
turns.text: Aggregate risk at the regulator level or provide a regulator-backed insurance layer for sandbox trading; it's easier than each start-up buying costly policies.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: Should the FCA provide a concierge service to help applicants?

turns.speaker: Chris Bosworth
turns.text: Yes—early collaborative dialogue with the eventual case officer would reduce wasted effort and repeated applications. Right now many firms hire ex-FCA consultants to bridge that gap.

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: Also keep and expand sandbox features that work—like the supercharged sandbox that provides compute and synthetic data for expensive tests—while fixing pathways to production.

chapters.title: Culture, competition and tech examples
chapters.takeaway: Regulatory culture feels cautious; better execution, openness and tech benchmarking would help. International programmes have been more active and the witnesses urged learning from them.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Fforestfach
turns.text: Is the regulator’s attitude 'guilty until proven innocent' and how to change it?

turns.speaker: Chris Bosworth
turns.text: There is suspicion. Large teams with bank experience often get trust; younger founders may struggle. More collaborative early phases would help.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: Do sandboxes mainly benefit big, known firms?

turns.speaker: Sebastian McDermott
turns.text: Many UK sandbox participants are established names. Frontier innovators have tended to go to programmes abroad where regulators are more active in tech assessment.

turns.speaker: Oliver Quie
turns.text: Examples from Singapore and the UAE show better execution: regulators placing sandboxes close to innovation hubs, running credible assessments, and making useful introductions.

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: Why did the FCA try to push Infact into the sandbox?

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: They didn't fully grasp our model; we needed industry-wide data access that a sandbox couldn't offer. The FCA told us we might be 'minded to refuse' unless we went into sandbox—yet later apologised and authorised us.

turns.speaker: Lord Smith of Kelvin
turns.text: Could sandbox confidentiality be abused by incumbents who copy ideas?

turns.speaker: Will Mason
turns.text: Confidentiality is maintained. But showcasing and PR around sandbox projects often favour well-known firms with resources to engage.

turns.speaker: Lord Hollick
turns.text: Oliver, your firm works on identifying actors in online trades. Could that have helped recent crypto exchange thefts?

turns.speaker: Oliver Quie
turns.text: Yes—we've worked with investigators on large crypto heists, tracing devices and geolocation. But crypto platforms often lack incentives to adopt strong authentication; regulation could change that.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We will close; your perspectives are a helpful counterpoint to previous evidence that celebrated sandboxes as a quick route to innovation.
